{{Short description|Result of commutative algebra}}
{{Use American English|date=March 2021}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=March 2021}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''Noether normalization lemma''' (sometimes referred to as a theorem rather than a lemma) is a result of [[commutative algebra]], introduced by [[Emmy Noether]] in 1926.<ref>{{harvnb|Noether|1926}}</ref> It states that for any [[Field (mathematics)|field]] <math>k</math>, and any [[Finitely generated algebra|finitely generated]] commutative [[algebra over a field|''k''-algebra]] <math>A</math>, there exist elements <math>y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_d</math> in <math>A</math> that are [[algebraically independent]] over <math>k</math> and such that <math>A</math> is a [[finitely generated module]] over the [[polynomial ring]] <math>S=k[y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_d]</math>. The integer <math>d</math> is equal to the [[Krull dimension]] of the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] <math>A</math>; and if <math>A</math> is an [[integral domain]], <math>d</math> is also the [[transcendence degree]] of the [[field of fractions]] of <math>A</math> over k.

The theorem has a geometric interpretation. Suppose ''A'' is the coordinate ring of an [[affine variety]] ''X'', and consider ''S'' as the [[coordinate ring]] of a ''d''-dimensional [[affine space]] <math>\mathbb A^d_k</math>.  Then the [[inclusion map]] <math>S\hookrightarrow A</math> induces a surjective [[finite morphism]] of [[affine varieties]] <math>X\to \mathbb A^d_k</math>: that is, any [[affine variety]] is a [[branched covering]] of affine space.
When ''k'' is infinite, such a branched [[Covering space|covering map]] can be constructed by taking a general projection from an affine space containing ''X'' to a ''d''-dimensional subspace.

More generally, in the language of [[scheme (mathematics)|scheme]]s, the theorem can equivalently be stated as: every affine ''k''-scheme (of [[scheme of finite type|finite type]]) ''X'' is [[finite morphism|finite]] over an affine ''n''-dimensional space. The theorem can be refined to include a [[chain (order theory)|chain]] of [[ideal of a ring|ideal]]s of ''R'' (equivalently, [[closed subset]]s of ''X'') that are finite over the affine coordinate subspaces of the corresponding dimensions.<ref name="Eisenbud">{{harvnb|Eisenbud|1995|loc=Theorem 13.3}}</ref>

The Noether normalization lemma yields [[Zariski's lemma]] as a corollary. In turn, Zariski's lemma can be used to give a straightforward proof of [[David Hilbert|Hilbert]]'s [[Nullstellensatz]], one of the most fundamental results of classical [[algebraic geometry]]. Noether normalization is also an important tool in establishing the notion of [[Krull dimension]] for ''k''-algebras.

== Statement and proof ==
'''Theorem.''' (''Noether Normalization Lemma'') Let ''k'' be a field and <math>A=k[y_1',...,y_m']</math> be a finitely generated ''k''-algebra.  Then for some integer ''d'', <math>0\leq d\leq m</math>, there exist <math>y_1,\ldots,y_d\in A</math> algebraically independent over ''k'' such that ''A'' is finite (i.e., finitely generated as a module) over <math>k[y_1,\ldots,y_d]</math> (the integer ''d'' is then equal to the Krull dimension of ''A''). If ''A'' is an integral domain, then ''d'' is also the transcendence degree of the field of fractions of ''A'' over ''k''.

The following proof is due to [[Masayoshi Nagata|Nagata]] and appears in [[David Mumford|Mumford]]'s ''Red Book''. A second, more geometric proof is given on page 176 of the same text. 

''Proof:'' We shall induct on ''m''. Case <math>m = 0</math> is <math>k=A</math> and there is nothing to prove. Assume <math>m=1</math>. Then <math>A\cong k[y]/I</math> as ''k''-algebras, where <math>I\subset k[y]</math> is some ideal. Since <math>k[y]</math> is a PID (it is a [[Euclidean domain]]), <math>I=(f)</math>. If <math>f=0</math> we are done, so assume <math>f\neq 0</math>. Let ''e'' be the degree of ''f''. Then ''A'' is generated, as a ''k''-[[vector space]], by <math>1,y,y^2,\dots,y^{e-1}</math>. Thus ''A'' is finite over ''k''. Assume now <math>m \geq 2</math>. If the <math>y_i'</math> are algebraically independent, then by setting <math>y_i=y_i'</math>, we are done.  If not, it is enough to prove the claim that there is a ''k''-subalgebra ''S'' of ''A'' that is generated by <math>m-1</math> elements, such that ''A'' is finite over ''S.'' Indeed, by the inductive hypothesis, we can find, for some integer ''d'', <math>0\leq d\leq m-1</math>, algebraically independent elements <math>y_1, ..., y_{d}</math> of ''S'' such that ''S'' is finite over <math>k[y_1, ..., y_d]</math>.  Since ''A'' is finite over ''S'', and ''S'' is finite over <math>k[y_1, ..., y_d]</math>, we obtain the desired conclusion that ''A'' is finite over <math>k[y_1, ..., y_d]</math>. 

To prove the claim, we assume by hypothesis that the <math>y_i'</math> are not algebraically independent, so that there is a nonzero polynomial ''f'' in ''m'' variables over ''k'' such that
:<math>f(y_1', \ldots, y_m') = 0</math>.
Given an integer ''r'' which is determined later, set
:<math>z_i = y_i' - (y_1')^{r^{i-1}}, \quad 2 \le i \le m,</math>
and, for simplification of notation, write <math>\tilde{y}=y_1'.</math>

Then the preceding reads:
:<math>f(\tilde{y}, z_2 + \tilde{y}^r, z_3 + \tilde{y}^{r^2}, \ldots, z_m + {\tilde{y}}^{r^{m-1}}) = 0.\ \ \ (*)</math>
Now, if <math>a \tilde{y}^{\alpha_1} \prod_2^m (z_i + {\tilde{y}}^{r^{i-1}})^{\alpha_i}</math> is a monomial appearing in the left-hand side of the above equation, with coefficient <math>a \in k</math>, the highest term in <math>\tilde{y}</math> after expanding the product looks like
:<math>a {\tilde{y}}^{\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 r + \cdots + \alpha_m r^{m-1}}</math>.
Whenever the above exponent agrees with the highest <math>\tilde{y}</math> exponent produced by some other monomial, it is possible that the highest term in <math>\tilde{y}</math> of <math>f(\tilde{y}, z_2 + \tilde{y}^r, z_3 + \tilde{y}^{r^2}, ..., z_m + {\tilde{y}}^{r^{m-1}})</math> will not be of the above form, because it may be affected by cancellation. However, if ''r'' is large enough (e.g., we can set <math>r = 1 + \deg f</math>), then each <math>\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 r + \cdots + \alpha_m r^{m-1}</math> encodes a unique base ''r'' number, so this does not occur. For such an ''r'', let <math>c\in k</math> be the coefficient of the unique monomial of ''f'' of multidegree <math>(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)</math> for which the quantity <math>\alpha_1 + \alpha_2 r + \cdots + \alpha_m r^{m-1}</math> is maximal. Multiplication of <math>(*)</math> by <math>1/c</math> gives an integral dependence equation of <math>\tilde{y}</math> over <math>S = k[z_2, ..., z_m]</math>, i.e., <math>y_1'(=\tilde{y})</math> is integral over ''S''.  Moreover, because <math>A=S[y_1']</math>, ''A'' is in fact finite over ''S.''  This completes the proof of the claim, so we are done with the first part.

Moreover, if ''A'' is an integral domain, then ''d'' is the transcendence degree of its field of fractions. Indeed, ''A'' and the polynomial ring <math>S = k[y_1, ..., y_d]</math> have the same transcendence degree (i.e., the degree of the field of fractions) since the field of fractions of ''A'' is algebraic over that of ''S'' (as ''A'' is integral over ''S'') and ''S'' has transcendence degree ''d''. Thus, it remains to show the Krull dimension of ''S'' is ''d''. (This is also a consequence of [[dimension theory (algebra)|dimension theory]].) We induct on ''d'', with the case <math>d=0</math> being trivial. Since <math>0 \subsetneq (y_1) \subsetneq (y_1, y_2) \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq (y_1, \dots, y_d)</math> is a chain of prime ideals, the dimension is at least ''d''. To get the reverse estimate, let <math>0 \subsetneq \mathfrak{p}_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq \mathfrak{p}_m</math> be a chain of prime ideals. Let <math>0 \ne u \in \mathfrak{p}_1</math>. We apply the Noether normalization and get <math>T = k[u, z_2, \dots, z_d]</math> (in the normalization process, we're free to choose the first variable) such that ''S'' is integral over ''T''. By the inductive hypothesis, <math>T/(u)</math> has dimension <math>d-1</math>. By [[Incomparability property (commutative algebra)|incomparability]], <math>\mathfrak{p}_i \cap T</math> is a chain of length <math>m</math> and then, in <math>T/(\mathfrak{p}_1 \cap T)</math>, it becomes a chain of length <math>m-1</math>. Since <math>\operatorname{dim} T/(\mathfrak{p}_1 \cap T) \le \operatorname{dim} T/(u)</math>, we have <math>m - 1 \le d - 1</math>. Hence, <math>\dim S \le d</math>. <math>\square</math>

== Refinement ==
The following refinement appears in Eisenbud's book, which builds on Nagata's idea:<ref name="Eisenbud" />
{{math_theorem
|Let ''A'' be a finitely generated algebra over a field ''k'', and <math>I_1 \subset \dots \subset I_m</math> be a chain of ideals such that <math>\operatorname{dim} (A/I_i) = d_i > d_{i+1}.</math> Then there exists algebraically independent elements ''y''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''y''<sub>''d''</sub> in ''A'' such that
# ''A'' is a finitely generated module over the polynomial subring ''S'' <nowiki>=</nowiki> ''k''[''y''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''y''<sub>''d''</sub>].
# <math>I_i \cap S = (y_{d_i+1}, \dots, y_d)</math>.
# If the <math>I_i</math>'s are homogeneous, then ''y''<sub>''i''</sub>'s may be taken to be homogeneous.
Moreover, if ''k'' is an infinite field, then ''any'' sufficiently general choice of ''y''<sub>''I''</sub>'s has Property 1 above ("sufficiently general" is made precise in the proof).}}
<!-- This refinement is useful; it says for example, that the ring ''A'' is a [[catenary ring]].-->

Geometrically speaking, the last part of the theorem says that for <math>X = \operatorname{Spec} A \subset \mathbf{A}^m</math> any general linear projection <math>\mathbf{A}^m \to \mathbf{A}^d</math> induces a [[finite morphism]] <math>X \to \mathbf{A}^d</math> (cf. the lede); besides Eisenbud, see also [https://arxiv.org/abs/1209.5993].

{{math_theorem|name=Corollary|Let ''A'' be an integral domain that is a finitely generated algebra over a field. If <math>\mathfrak{p}</math> is a prime ideal of ''A'', then
:<math>\dim A = \operatorname{height} \mathfrak{p} + \dim A/\mathfrak{p}</math>.
In particular, the Krull dimension of the localization of ''A'' at ''any'' maximal ideal is dim ''A''.}}

{{math_theorem|name=Corollary|Let <math>A \subset B</math> be integral domains that are finitely generated algebras over a field. Then
:<math>\dim B = \dim A + \operatorname{tr.deg}_{Q(A)} Q(B)</math>
(the special case of [[Nagata's altitude formula]]).}}

== Illustrative application: generic freeness ==
A typical nontrivial application of the normalization lemma is the [[generic freeness]] theorem: Let <math>A, B</math> be rings such that <math>A</math> is a Noetherian integral domain and suppose there is a [[ring homomorphism]] <math>A \to B</math> that exhibits <math>B</math> as a finitely generated algebra over <math>A</math>. Then there is some <math>0 \ne g \in A</math> such that <math>B[g^{-1}]</math> is a free <math>A[g^{-1}]</math>-module.

To prove this, let <math>F</math> be the [[fraction field]] of <math>A</math>. We argue by induction on the Krull dimension of <math>F \otimes_A B</math>. The base case is when the Krull dimension is <math>-\infty</math>; i.e., <math>F \otimes_A B = 0</math>; that is, when there is some <math>0 \ne g \in A</math> such that <math>g B = 0</math> , so that <math>B[g^{-1}]</math> is free as an <math>A[g^{-1}]</math>-module. For the inductive step, note that <math>F \otimes_A B</math> is a finitely generated <math>F</math>-algebra. Hence by the Noether normalization lemma, <math>F \otimes_A B</math> contains algebraically independent elements <math>x_1, \dots, x_d</math> such that <math>F \otimes_A B</math> is finite over the polynomial ring <math>F[x_1, \dots, x_d]</math>. Multiplying each <math>x_i</math> by elements of <math>A</math>, we can assume <math>x_i</math> are in <math>B</math>. We now consider:
:<math>A' := A[x_1, \dots, x_d] \to B.</math>
Now <math>B</math> may not be finite over <math>A'</math>, but it will become finite after inverting a single element as follows. If <math>b</math> is an element of <math>B</math>, then, as an element of <math>F \otimes_A B</math>, it is integral over <math>F[x_1, \dots, x_d]</math>; i.e., <math>b^n + a_1 b^{n-1} + \dots + a_n = 0</math> for some <math>a_i</math> in <math>F[x_1, \dots, x_d]</math>. Thus, some <math>0 \ne g \in A</math> kills all the denominators of the coefficients of <math>a_i</math> and so <math>b</math> is integral over <math>A'[g^{-1}]</math>. Choosing some finitely many generators of <math>B</math> as an <math>A'</math>-algebra and applying this observation to each generator, we find some <math>0 \ne g \in A</math> such that <math>B[g^{-1}]</math> is integral (thus finite) over <math>A'[g^{-1}]</math>. Replace <math>B, A</math> by <math>B[g^{-1}], A[g^{-1}]</math> and then we can assume <math>B</math> is finite over <math>A' := A[x_1, \dots, x_d]</math>.
To finish, consider a finite filtration <math>B = B_0 \supset B_1 \supset B_2 \supset \cdots \supset B_r</math> by <math>A'</math>-submodules such that <math>B_i / B_{i+1} \simeq A'/\mathfrak{p}_i</math> for prime ideals <math>\mathfrak{p}_i</math> (such a filtration exists by the theory of [[associated prime]]s). For each ''i'', if <math>\mathfrak{p}_i \ne 0</math>, by inductive hypothesis, we can choose some <math>g_i \ne 0</math> in <math>A</math> such that <math>A'/\mathfrak{p}_i[g_i^{-1}]</math> is free as an <math>A[g_i^{-1}]</math>-module, while <math>A'</math> is a polynomial ring and thus free. Hence, with <math>g = g_0 \cdots g_r</math>, <math>B[g^{-1}]</math> is a [[free module]] over <math>A[g^{-1}]</math>. <math>\square</math>
